transcript.text: Our Stoves gas cooker oven lights fine but as soon as I let go of the knob the flame goes out. Hob burners all fine. It's a Richmond something, freestanding. Is this a DIY job?

That symptom is very commonly the oven flame-failure device/thermocouple not proving that there’s a flame.

The oven lights while you are holding the knob in because the gas valve is manually held open. Once released, the safety device should stay energised from the heat of the flame; if it does not, it shuts the gas off. The hob burners being fine does not rule this out — they have separate controls/safety devices.

Before calling someone, try the simple check:

1. Light the oven as normal, with the knob fully depressed.
2. Keep it held in for 15–30 seconds after the flame has lit (some take longer from cold).
3. Release it slowly.
4. Check that the oven flame is actually reaching the small metal probe beside the burner (the thermocouple). A weak, uneven or displaced flame can prevent it heating properly.

If it still goes out, likely causes are:

• failed or loose thermocouple;
• faulty oven gas-valve/flame-failure solenoid;
• burner/jet issue giving a poor flame around the sensor.

It is often a fairly routine repair for an engineer, but I would not recommend DIY work on the oven gas valve, thermocouple connections or burner assembly unless you are properly competent and following the manufacturer’s service information. For a UK appliance, use a Gas Safe registered engineer (ideally one experienced with Stoves/Richmond cookers). Have the full model and serial number from the rating plate ready — usually around the oven door frame, drawer area, or rear of the cooker.

Don’t bypass or wedge the knob in, and don’t attempt to defeat the safety device. If you smell gas, turn the appliance off, ventilate the room, avoid switches/flames, and contact the gas emergency service or an engineer.

Thank you. I tried holding it in for 15, 20 and 30 seconds and it still goes out when I let go. The flame looks mostly blue but a bit weaker at the end near the little probe. I only smell gas briefly while I'm trying to light it, and the CO alarm in the kitchen hasn't sounded.

A brief whiff of gas while it is sparking and then immediately lights can be normal. It should stop as soon as the flame is established. A CO alarm will not normally detect unburned natural gas/LPG, so it does not confirm that there is no gas leak — it is for carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion.

Given that the flame is weaker at the thermocouple/probe end, the most likely possibilities are:

• a partly blocked burner port near the probe;
• the burner or probe is slightly out of position;
• a failing thermocouple; or
• less commonly, the oven flame-failure valve.

You can do a limited non-gas DIY check only when the cooker is fully cold and isolated from electricity:

• Consult the cooker manual for removal of the oven base plate/flame spreader, if designed to be user-removable.
• Vacuum/brush away loose debris from the burner area and holes/slots near the probe.
• Make sure the burner is seated properly and the probe has not been bent away from the flame.
• Do not poke wire, pins or drills into the jet/injector or enlarge burner holes, and do not loosen any gas fittings or thermocouple connections.

If cleaning/reseating the accessible burner does not give a firm blue flame that heats the probe, book a Gas Safe engineer. A thermocouple replacement is usually not a major repair, but it involves safety-critical gas components and should be diagnosed properly.

Until then, don’t use the oven or try to hold/wedge the control knob in. The hob can generally still be used if it lights normally and there is no continuing gas smell. If gas smell persists after turning controls off, turn off the appliance/gas supply if safe to do so, ventilate, avoid electrical switches or flames, and call the gas emergency service.
